title: Look at the bits, legally
description:
Reading a `float`'s bytes through an `int*` breaks the *strict aliasing* rule: the compiler is allowed to assume a `float` and an `int` never occupy the same memory, and to optimise on that basis.

`std::bit_cast` (C++20, in `<bit>`) does the same job correctly: it produces a new object of another type with the same bits.

Rewrite both functions with `std::bit_cast`:

- `std::uint32_t bitsOf(float value)`
- `bool isNegative(float value)`: true when the sign bit (the top bit) is set. This is true for `-0.0f` as well, which `value < 0` would miss.
unitTests:
TEST("bitsOf") { CHECK_EQ(bitsOf(1.0f), 0x3F800000u); CHECK_EQ(bitsOf(0.0f), 0u); CHECK_EQ(bitsOf(-2.0f), 0xC0000000u); }
TEST("isNegative reads the sign bit") { CHECK(isNegative(-1.5f)); CHECK(!isNegative(1.5f)); CHECK(!isNegative(0.0f)); CHECK(isNegative(-0.0f)); }

grading.unitTests:
TEST("bitsOf") { CHECK_EQ(bitsOf(1.0f), 0x3F800000u); CHECK_EQ(bitsOf(0.0f), 0u); CHECK_EQ(bitsOf(-2.0f), 0xC0000000u); }
